take_homes: A flat score tells you the measure is exhausted, not that the work is good. Check the judge against your own verdicts on a few outputs before trusting it.
Being correct and being useful are separate standards. Someone has to write down what good means, and that stays a human and leadership job.
Whether an agent may send something is a design decision about the loop, and some categories never go without a person.

monday.move: Write a one-paragraph standard for what a good people-update mail looks like, and draft the question 'which of our outputs would we ever let go out without a human reading them?' for the leadership team agenda.
monday.who: Me, then one HR business partner to react to it
monday.when: Monday morning for the draft; the leadership team item at the next meeting
monday.stop_condition: If the HR partner can't tell the good example from the bad one using my standard, I rewrite it before going further
monday.blocker: Anything involving employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO first, and I still haven't asked them. So I only use non-personal example mails.

misconception.why: The module says people move up to designing the loop and owning the standard, and that some categories always need a human. It still never answers which roles go, and I did not hear anything about the people who currently do the checking. So I still think headcount is the real question. I just no longer think 'replace' is the only framing.

one_line: Good on 'who decides what good means' and 'don't trust a flat score'. Heavy on tool mechanics, and it never says what happens to the people whose job was checking.
